title: The Science Behind Why Mosquitoes Bite Some People More Than Others
excerpt: From skin chemistry to beer consumption, researchers are unraveling the complex cocktail of signals that make certain people irresistible to the world's deadliest animal.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mosquitoes are attracted to specific skin compounds, not just blood type.
  • Beer drinkers are 1.35 times more appealing to Anopheles mosquitoes.
  • Climate change is expanding mosquito habitats, increasing disease risks.
  • Genetics account for 85% of mosquito attraction factors in individuals.
  • Scientists have identified 27 odorous compounds — out of roughly 1,000 produced by the human body — that mosquitoes actively detect when choosing a host.
  • Skin chemistry, particularly carboxylic acids and a sebum breakdown product called "mushroom alcohol," plays a larger role than blood type, which researchers now say has weak scientific backing.
  • A 2026 preprint study of 465 people found beer drinkers were 1.35 times more attractive to Anopheles mosquitoes, while a separate study showed the insects can learn to associate DEET repellent with food.
  • Climate change is expanding mosquito ranges into new regions, raising stakes for disease transmission of malaria, dengue, Zika and chikungunya worldwide.

If you have ever been devoured by mosquitoes while the person next to you walked away unscathed, science confirms you are not imagining it. A growing body of research is decoding the precise chemical signals that make certain humans irresistible to mosquitoes — and the answers go far beyond old wives' tales about "sweet blood."

"It's not a misconception — mosquitoes are attracted to some people more than others," Frederic Simard, a medical entomologist at France's Institute of Research for Development, told AFP. "But we are not all magnets all the time."

How Mosquitoes Hunt You Down

Female mosquitoes — the only ones that bite — deploy a layered detection system to find hosts. Carbon dioxide exhaled by humans is the first trigger, detectable from dozens of meters away. "We have known for over 100 years that mosquitoes are attracted by the carbon dioxide that we exhale — this is the first signal that triggers their behavior," Swedish scientist Rickard Ignell told AFP.

Within about 10 meters, body odor kicks in. Ignell's recent study, published in Nature, released Aedes aegypti mosquitoes on 42 women in a lab and identified 27 odorous compounds — out of roughly 1,000 humans produce — that the insects actively detect. The women mosquitoes preferred most produced elevated levels of a compound called 1-octen-3-ol, also known as "mushroom alcohol," a breakdown product of the skin oil sebum.

"Mosquitoes will start detecting our odor, and in combination with carbon dioxide, this attracts them even more."

— Rickard Ignell, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences

At close range, body temperature and humidity seal the deal. A 2020 study published in Science found that disabling a molecular thermostat in mosquito antennae reduced their ability to detect warmth, though the insects could still rely on other cues.

Blood Type, Beer and Bad News About DEET

The popular belief that Type O blood attracts more mosquitoes rests on thin evidence. A 2004 study found mosquitoes landed on Type O individuals nearly twice as often as those with Type A, but Simard was blunt: the idea "has no scientific basis" given the small sample sizes involved. Skin-derived carboxylic acids — compounds found in sweat and generated by skin microbes — appear to matter far more. A 2022 Rockefeller University study found that people producing higher levels of these acids were consistently more attractive to mosquitoes, and that this trait remained stable over time.

What you drink may also matter. A 2026 preprint study tracked 465 volunteers at a music festival in the Netherlands and found that those who had consumed beer in the previous 24 hours were 1.35 times more attractive to Anopheles mosquitoes. Researchers attributed this partly to changes in skin odor rather than blood alcohol levels alone, according to Healthline.

Perhaps most unsettling, a study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology found that mosquitoes can learn to associate the smell of DEET — long considered the gold standard repellent — with food. After repeated exposure alongside warm blood, more than 60% of trained mosquitoes attempted to feed when presented only with DEET's scent.

"The mosquito's brain can rewrite that response based on experience. What the insect has learned matters just as much as what the chemical does."

— Clément Vinauger, Associate Professor of Biochemistry, Virginia Tech

Research studies and expert interviews

Roughly 85% of what makes a person more or less attractive to mosquitoes is hardwired into their DNA, according to Timothy Winegard, author of The Mosquito: A Human History of Our Deadliest Predator. This genetic influence expresses itself through skin bacteria composition, metabolic rate, natural body temperature and the unique cocktail of compounds each person's skin emits. Pregnant women, for instance, exhale about 21% more carbon dioxide and run about 1.26 degrees Fahrenheit warmer around the belly, attracting roughly twice as many bites from malaria-carrying species, according to multiple studies cited by Smithsonian Magazine.

Even clothing color plays a role. A 2022 University of Washington study found that Aedes aegypti mosquitoes are drawn to red, orange, black and cyan — colors that correspond to longer wavelengths, similar to those emitted by human skin. Green, purple, blue and white were largely ignored.

Rising Stakes as Mosquitoes Spread

Understanding mosquito preferences has taken on new urgency as climate change expands the insects' range. The tiger mosquito, a vector for the chikungunya virus, has pushed into new territories, reaching France's Alsace region for the first time in 2025. In the United States, West Nile virus cases are spreading at the fastest rate in 20 years, with 56 cases reported across multiple states as of mid-July 2026, according to the CDC.

"Mosquitoes are said to be the most dangerous animals on our planet because they can transmit serious infections, including malaria, yellow fever, Zika, dengue, and chikungunya," said William Schaffner, professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt University, in an interview with Healthline.

For the Indian diaspora, the stakes cut both ways. India bears one of the world's heaviest burdens of mosquito-borne diseases — the country recorded over 60,000 dengue cases and hundreds of malaria deaths in recent years, with monsoon season driving peak transmission. Indians traveling between the US, Europe and India navigate shifting mosquito risks in both directions as warming temperatures redraw the map of where these diseases thrive.

What You Can Do

Experts recommend loose-fitting, light-colored clothing that covers skin, along with regular reapplication of DEET-based repellents rather than a single heavy dose. Fans directed at the feet and ankles — where odor-producing skin bacteria congregate — can also help, according to Harvard Health. Simard's advice was more direct: "Try to eat light meals — and go easy on the alcohol."
